subject: se
name: The Software Engineering Project · Set B

questions.stem: Which requirement is fully SMART?
options: "The dashboard shall render within 2 seconds for 95% of requests on a 4G connection, by the pilot release"
"The system should load quickly for most users"
"The system will use a modern front-end framework"
"Users will find the system easy to learn"
questions.explanation: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound — and therefore testable later, which is the point of SMART.

questions.stem: The distinction between a functional and a performance requirement is that functional requirements state:
options: How well the system must operate
The acceptance criteria for sign-off
The technologies to be used
What the system must do
questions.explanation: "Users can cancel a booking" is functional; "cancellation confirms within 2 seconds under load" is performance.

questions.stem: A project boundary differs from a boundary value because the project boundary:
options: Is a value at the edge of a valid input range
Sets the maximum budget
Marks the deadline for delivery
Separates the system being built from everything outside it, defining scope
questions.explanation: The same word carries a different meaning in testing — the deliberate overlap is examinable.

questions.stem: Feasibility in this course is assessed against:
options: Technical novelty and market demand
Whether the client has approved the design
Whether the required technology exists anywhere
Whether the project can realistically be completed within the available schedule and budget
questions.explanation: Schedule and budget are the two named dimensions — an answer ignoring either is incomplete.

questions.stem: A use case documents:
options: The actor, trigger, main sequence and alternative or error paths for achieving a goal
The database schema for a feature
The tasks and their dependencies
The classes and their relationships
questions.explanation: The error paths matter as much as the main sequence — they become both requirements and test cases.

questions.stem: Missing a stakeholder most typically causes:
options: A verification failure at unit testing
A merge conflict during integration
A performance shortfall under load
A validation failure — the system matches its specification but not the real need
questions.explanation: It surfaces only when real users encounter the finished product, which is why it is expensive.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart's bar length encodes:
options: The task's importance
The number of people assigned
The task's duration
The percentage complete
questions.explanation: Duration — Percentage complete is usually shaded within the bar, and dependencies are shown by links between bars.

questions.stem: A task with two weeks of float is delayed three weeks. The project end date:
options: Is unaffected
Slips by two weeks
Slips by three weeks
Slips by one week, as the task is now critical
questions.explanation: Float absorbs delay only up to its length — the arithmetic is exactly what a stimulus question tests.

questions.stem: The critical path is best defined as:
options: The longest chain of dependent tasks, determining the minimum project duration
The most expensive sequence of tasks
The tasks with the highest risk rating
The tasks assigned to the most experienced staff
questions.explanation: Criticality comes from dependency and duration, not from cost, risk or seniority.

questions.stem: A collaboration tool's principal project benefit is:
options: A single source of truth with version history and a visible audit trail of decisions
Eliminating the need for status meetings
Automatic generation of the Gantt chart
Guaranteed data security for project files
questions.explanation: Named risks are tool sprawl, notification overload, access control and dependence on connectivity.

questions.stem: Which process diary entry best evidences EC-style ongoing evaluation?
options: "Login page complete. Usability check with two students showed the error message was missed; moved it inline beside the field and re-tested — both found it immediately."
"Completed the login page today."
"Spent four hours on the login page."
"Login page finished ahead of schedule."
questions.explanation: Activity, evaluation against a criterion, the resulting change, and re-verification — the full loop in one entry.

questions.stem: A budget omitting licence renewals and hosting will:
options: Understate lifetime cost and may lead to selecting the wrong option
Be rejected by the client automatically
Prevent the Gantt chart from being completed
Breach accounting standards
questions.explanation: Ongoing operating cost frequently dominates the comparison between a cheaper build and a cheaper run.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an approach to a project characteristic?
options: Waterfall — requirements evolving weekly
Agile — a fixed-price regulated project requiring full up-front specification
Prototyping — requirements unclear and the interface is central
End-user development — a public-facing payments system
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are each matched to the condition that most argues against them, and (D) applies a low-governance approach to a high-risk system.

questions.stem: WAgile is best described as:
options: A testing methodology combining black and white box techniques
An implementation method between phased and parallel
A hybrid applying Waterfall's structured planning with Agile iteration at defined points
A version control branching strategy
questions.explanation: It suits organisations needing up-front approval and documentation while wanting iterative delivery inside phases.

questions.stem: Scrum's fixed-length iteration is bracketed by:
options: A design review and a code freeze
A stand-up and a retrospective only
Sprint planning at the start, and a review plus retrospective at the end
A backlog grooming session and a release
questions.explanation: Kanban has none of these — it is continuous flow governed by WIP limits.

questions.stem: A Kanban WIP limit exists to:
options: Restrict how many items are in progress at once, exposing bottlenecks
Cap the project budget
Set the length of each iteration
Limit the number of developers on the team
questions.explanation: It replaces the sprint boundary as the mechanism that forces work to finish before more is started.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the product backlog from the sprint backlog?
options: The product backlog contains only the current iteration's committed work
The product backlog is fixed once agreed and cannot be reprioritised
The product backlog is maintained by the developers without client input
The product backlog holds all outstanding work, from which a slice is drawn for the sprint
questions.explanation: Reprioritisation is the point — a backlog that cannot change defeats the purpose of iterating.

questions.stem: A Level 0 DFD deliberately omits:
options: External entities
Data stores
Data flows
The system process
questions.explanation: Level 0 shows the whole system as one process with its external entities and net flows; data stores appear from Level 1.

questions.stem: Balancing between DFD levels means that:
options: Each process is decomposed to equal depth
Each level contains the same number of data stores
The external inputs and outputs crossing the boundary are identical at both levels
Processes are numbered consecutively
questions.explanation: A new external input at Level 1 means the scope changed — which must be resolved rather than drawn.

questions.stem: Which is a valid DFD connection?
options: Process → data store
External entity → data store
Data store → data store
External entity → external entity
questions.explanation: All movement of data passes through a process — the other three are the standard connection errors.

questions.stem: A DFD process labelled "Customer" rather than "Process Order" is incorrect because processes are named:
options: With the responsible department
With their level number only
With the data they consume
With a verb and object
questions.explanation: Nouns belong on data stores and external entities; a noun on a process usually signals a modelling error.

questions.stem: In a structure chart, an arrow with an open circle typically denotes:
options: A data item passed between modules
A control flag
A module boundary
An external entity
questions.explanation: A filled circle denotes a control flag — the two markers are distinguished by fill, which is easy to lose in a hand-drawn answer.

questions.stem: A class diagram's inheritance arrow points:
options: From the parent to the subclass, with a filled diamond
From the subclass to the parent, with a hollow triangle
Between any two classes, with a dashed line
From the subclass to the parent, with an open arrowhead
questions.explanation: Direction and head shape both matter — markers reward correct standard notation explicitly.

questions.stem: Which artefact best communicates a screen sequence to a non-technical client?
options: A Level 1 DFD
A structure chart
A storyboard
A class diagram
questions.explanation: It exposes missing steps in the journey while change still costs nothing, and needs no notation knowledge to read.

questions.stem: A data dictionary documents each field's:
options: Position on the user interface
Encryption algorithm and key length
Name, type, size or format, validation rules and purpose
Frequency of update
questions.explanation: It is technical documentation aimed at whoever maintains the system later.

questions.stem: Pseudocode's advantage over code for design review is that it:
options: Expresses logic in language-neutral form so reviewers assess the algorithm rather than syntax
Executes without a compiler
Automatically generates the implementation
Documents the database schema
questions.explanation: The 2025 paper asked candidates to convert pseudocode to Python — the two directions test different skills.

questions.stem: Which activity is design thinking rather than computational thinking?
options: Interviewing users and building empathy maps
Decomposing the system into modules
Designing an efficient sorting algorithm
Choosing an appropriate data structure
questions.explanation: Computational thinking makes it work, design thinking makes it usable, systems thinking makes it fit.

questions.stem: Recognising that a new rostering system will change payroll, leave management and reporting is:
options: Computational thinking
Systems thinking
Design thinking
Agile planning
questions.explanation: Interdependencies, feedback loops and unintended consequences are its named concerns.

questions.stem: Which activity is not a named contribution of back-end engineering to a project?
options: Appropriate technology selection
Robust error handling so the system fails gracefully
Wireframing the user journey
Security engineering protecting the whole system
questions.explanation: The fourth named contribution is interfacing with the front end through a well-designed API or data contract.

questions.stem: Quality assurance differs from testing because QA:
options: Occurs only at the end of the project
Defines measurable criteria and checks continually against requirements throughout development
Is performed exclusively by the client
Applies only to documentation
questions.explanation: Testing detects defects; QA is the surrounding process that keeps the work aligned to the requirements.

questions.stem: Which requirements tool is strongest for quantifying priorities across many stakeholders?
options: In-depth interviews
A presentation of research results
A prototype
A survey
questions.explanation: Interviews buy depth and context; surveys buy breadth and comparability. Using both is the strong answer.

questions.stem: A prototype's characteristic risk is that:
options: Users cannot provide meaningful feedback on incomplete software
It cannot be used for UI-heavy systems
Users mistake it for a finished product and fixate on visuals over function
It removes the need for requirements gathering
questions.explanation: Keeping early prototypes deliberately low fidelity is the standard mitigation.

questions.stem: Presenting research results to stakeholders is valuable primarily because it:
options: Surfaces disagreement early and secures decisions and funding
Demonstrates the amount of work completed
Replaces the need for written documentation
Shortens the requirements phase
questions.explanation: Its value lies in the disagreement it exposes rather than the approval it collects.

questions.stem: Direct implementation is characterised by:
options: Highest safety at highest cost
Fastest and cheapest, with no fallback if the new system fails
A staged rollout by module
A trial with one group before wider release
questions.explanation: The decision turns on consequence of failure, which is why it suits low-stakes internal tools.

questions.stem: Parallel implementation's defining benefit is:
options: The old system remains available as a fallback and outputs can be cross-checked
It requires no staff training
It completes the transition fastest
It limits risk to a single site
questions.explanation: (D) describes pilot — the four methods are distinguished by exactly this kind of detail.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain trials a new stock system in one store before national rollout. This is:
options: Direct
Phased
Parallel
Pilot
questions.explanation: Pilot — Its weakness is that the trial site may not represent the wider organisation.

questions.stem: Phased implementation's characteristic cost is:
options: Temporary interfaces between old and new modules over a long transition
Doubled data entry across the organisation
No fallback if the cutover fails
An unrepresentative trial population
questions.explanation: Risk is contained per module and training is spread, at the price of duration and interim complexity.

questions.stem: Which conversion method is most defensible for a payroll system?
options: Direct, to minimise cost
Parallel, given irreplaceable data and legal obligations
Pilot in one department
Phased over 12 months
questions.explanation: The cost of double entry is trivial relative to the consequence of staff not being paid correctly.

questions.stem: A stub is used in testing to:
options: Stand in for a module the code under test calls
Call the module under test from above
Generate randomised test inputs
Record test outcomes automatically
questions.explanation: A driver does (B) — the two are complements and are routinely swapped in answers.

questions.stem: Verification asks whether the team is:
options: Building the right system for the user's need
Building the system right against the specification
Building it within budget
Building it to an accessible standard
questions.explanation: Validation asks (A) — a system can pass verification and fail validation when the specification itself was wrong.

questions.stem: Which testing level assumes the components already pass in isolation?
options: Unit
Path
Black box
Integration
questions.explanation: Integration — It checks that modules and external systems exchange data correctly, which presupposes each works alone.

questions.stem: White box testing is distinguished by:
options: Designing tests to exercise specific internal paths, branches and loops
Checking outputs for given inputs without seeing the code
Testing performed by end users
Testing the system against the original requirements
questions.explanation: Path testing is a white box technique — you cannot design path coverage without seeing the code.

questions.stem: For a field accepting 1–100, which values are extreme rather than boundary?
options: "abc" and a blank entry
questions.explanation: Extreme data is far beyond the expected range and confirms the system does not crash; (C) is abnormal/invalid data.

questions.stem: Abnormal test data confirms that:
options: Typical operation is correct
Invalid input is rejected gracefully with a helpful message
Performance targets are met
Every logical path executes
questions.explanation: A crash on abnormal input is a defect and frequently a vulnerability — SQL injection strings belong in this category.

questions.stem: A test case without a documented expected result:
options: Cannot be automated
Cannot be traced to a requirement
Is invalid only for boundary data
Cannot meaningfully pass or fail, since there is nothing to compare against
questions.explanation: Comparing actual with expected is the fundamental test of correctness.

questions.stem: Using de-identified production data in a sandbox rather than live production data:
options: Removes the ability to find real-world anomalies
Retains realistic messiness while removing privacy exposure and corruption risk
Requires the data to be regenerated for each test
Prevents boundary testing
questions.explanation: It is the standard compromise between simulated data's safety and live data's realism.

questions.stem: A logic error is distinguished from a runtime error because it:
options: Runs to completion and produces the wrong result
Prevents the program from starting
Is reported by the interpreter with a traceback
Occurs only in loops
questions.explanation: Nothing reports it, which is what makes it the hardest of the three categories to find.

questions.stem: Debugging differs from testing because debugging:
options: Establishes that a defect exists
Locates and fixes the cause of a defect already detected
Is performed before any code is written
Is conducted by the client
questions.explanation: Reading the traceback, adding print statements, using breakpoints and isolating with a minimal test case are the named techniques.

questions.stem: Adaptive maintenance responds to:
options: A defect reported by users
A request for an additional feature
A changed environment such as a new OS version or new legislation
Proactive refactoring before problems occur
questions.explanation: Corrective fixes defects, perfective enhances and preventive refactors — all four appear as options here.

questions.stem: Which is perfective maintenance?
options: Patching a dependency before a vulnerability is exploited
Improving report generation speed at the client's request
Correcting a miscalculated total
Updating the system for a new tax rate
questions.explanation: (A) is preventive, (C) corrective and (D) adaptive — the four categories are examined as a set.

questions.stem: A client adds three features mid-project with no change to time or budget. The professional response is:
options: Absorb the work to protect the relationship
Document the time and cost impact, present options — extend, re-prioritise or defer — and obtain written agreement
Decline without explanation
Deliver them by shortening the testing phase
questions.explanation: Change is legitimate; unpriced and unapproved change is what damages projects. (D) is how projects fail quietly.

questions.stem: A team adopts Agile but the client cannot attend reviews. The likely outcome is:
options: The core benefit of validated feedback is lost, and the team iterates on assumptions
Faster delivery through fewer interruptions
Improved documentation quality
Reduced defect rates
questions.explanation: Method selection must account for the client's capacity, not only the team's preference.

questions.stem: A system passes every unit and integration test but staff say it does not fit their workflow. The root cause lies in:
options: Requirements gathered from the wrong stakeholders during identifying and defining
Insufficient regression testing
Poor code quality
An inappropriate conversion method
questions.explanation: It is a validation failure — the build is correct against a specification that did not reflect the real need.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart shows all development complete but no testing has started. The most likely explanation is:
options: The project is genuinely finished
The critical path excluded testing legitimately
The float was miscalculated
Testing was never scheduled as work with duration and owners
questions.explanation: Testing and evaluating is a project stage, not something that happens after "the work".

questions.stem: The strongest evidence of managed development for a marker is:
options: A polished finished product
A comprehensive final report
Extensive inline code comments
Planned versus actual on time and scope, a decision log with reasoning, and version control history
questions.explanation: Planned versus actual demonstrates that development was managed rather than merely occurring.

questions.stem: A prototype's polish causes the client to believe the project is nearly complete. The best mitigation is:
options: Stop demonstrating prototypes
Provide a numeric completion percentage instead
Increase the polish so the client sees the real quality
Set expectations explicitly about what is simulated, and keep early prototypes low fidelity
questions.explanation: (C) worsens it — the more finished it looks, the stronger the false impression.

questions.stem: A team proposes cutting documentation to hit a deadline. The strongest counter is:
options: Documentation is legally mandated for all software
Documentation improves runtime performance
Maintenance dominates lifetime cost, and undocumented systems create key-person dependency and rework
The client will read the documentation carefully
questions.explanation: The saving is realised once; the cost recurs for as long as the system is maintained.

questions.stem: "The lead developer may leave" is best treated by:
options: Purchasing insurance
Cross-training, documentation and shared ownership of components
Increasing the contingency budget
Reducing the project scope
questions.explanation: Key-person dependency is reduced by changing how the team works, not by financial transfer.

questions.stem: A new system substantially changes daily workflows. The dominant operational risk is:
options: Insufficient database indexing
Excessive float on the critical path
User resistance and inadequate training causing disruption at cutover
Poor choice of front-end framework
questions.explanation: Treated through change management, early involvement, super-users, timely training and a safer conversion method.

questions.stem: A post-implementation review is most valuable when it:
options: Identifies who was responsible for defects
Confirms the client's satisfaction
Closes the project budget
Measures achievement against the original success criteria and captures lessons for the next project
questions.explanation: Scheduling it with a date in the implementation plan is what makes it happen at all.

questions.stem: A client requests delivery in 6 weeks for work realistically needing 16. The best response is:
options: Agree and manage expectations later
Compress testing and documentation to fit
Decline the project outright
Present the evidence-based estimate and offer a reduced-scope deliverable in 6 weeks with a phased roadmap
questions.explanation: Negotiate scope, not quality — which maps directly onto MoSCoW prioritisation.

questions.stem: For an outsourced build, the most consequential commonly omitted term is:
options: The vendor's office location
The choice of programming language
The number of developers assigned
Exit and transition arrangements
questions.explanation: Vendor lock-in is realised at the moment you try to leave, which is precisely when it cannot be renegotiated.

questions.stem: Which best demonstrates ongoing rather than end-of-project evaluation?
options: Iteration-by-iteration assessment against criteria, with recorded consequent changes
A final report after go-live
A single UAT session before sign-off
A client satisfaction survey at handover
questions.explanation: Evaluation that changes nothing is documentation — the record of consequent change is what makes it evaluation.

questions.stem: Users make frequent errors despite the system meeting every requirement. The correct reading is:
options: The users require more training and the design is sound
The requirements were over-specified
Persistent error is a design signal — usability test, modify under change control, then regression test
The error rate is within normal tolerance
questions.explanation: "Modifying designs to improve functionality" is an explicit part of testing and evaluating.

questions.stem: Which artefact suits a maintainer audience?
options: Technical documentation with DFDs, ERD, data dictionary and commented code
An infographic explaining the system's purpose
A quick-reference card for daily tasks
A short demonstration video
questions.explanation: Match the artefact to the audience — executives get benefits, cost and risk; end users get training material.

questions.stem: A team schedules integration testing before all modules exist. This is possible because of:
options: Stubs and drivers
Regression testing
Path testing
Boundary analysis
questions.explanation: They decouple testing from build order, which is what lets testing start early rather than pile up at the end.

questions.stem: A defect fix is shipped without re-running the existing suite. The risk is:
options: A compilation failure
A merge conflict on the next commit
An outdated data dictionary
A regression that nothing is watching for
questions.explanation: The fix is verified; the surrounding behaviour is not — which is exactly what regression testing covers.

questions.stem: A traceability matrix demonstrates:
options: That every risk has an owner
That every task has a dependency
That every requirement has a test and a recorded result
That every class has a parent
questions.explanation: It is the direct evidence for the functionality criterion in an evaluation.

questions.stem: Which is a measurable evaluation criterion?
options: "The system is intuitive"
"The interface follows modern design conventions"
"Staff appear satisfied"
"Median time to complete a booking is under 60 seconds and the double-booking rate is 0%"
questions.explanation: Evaluation must return to the measurable criteria set in the problem definition — closing that loop is what earns marks.

questions.stem: The strongest structure for an evaluation answer is:
options: Describe each feature and its purpose
Criterion → evidence → judgement → limitation → recommendation
List the technologies used and why they were chosen
Compare the solution with a commercial alternative
questions.explanation: Description without judgement is the single most common way to lose marks on an 8-mark question.

questions.stem: A student project claims Agile was used. The strongest supporting evidence is:
options: Sprint records showing planned versus delivered increments, feedback received and backlog changes made
A statement in the report that Agile was chosen
A single Gantt chart covering the whole project
A list of the twelve Agile principles
questions.explanation: Evidence of the practice, not the label — (C) would tend to suggest the opposite.

questions.stem: Which is the best reason to write the test plan before the code?
options: Designing tests forces the question "how would we know?", exposing ambiguous requirements early
It shortens the total project duration
It allows testing to be outsourced
It reduces the number of tests required
questions.explanation: It is the same shift-left logic that drives early prototyping and stakeholder involvement.

questions.stem: A project delivers on time and on budget but the original problem persists. The correct assessment is:
options: Failure on the criterion that matters — the measurable outcome in the problem definition
Success, since the constraints were met
Partial success, pending a revised problem definition
Success, provided the client signed off
questions.explanation: Time and budget are constraints; the objective is the outcome. Meeting the first while missing the second is a documented pattern.

questions.stem: The clearest sign of scope creep is:
options: The client has requested a change
The Gantt chart has been revised
Delivered functionality has grown without corresponding change to time, budget or documented agreement
A new risk has been added to the register
questions.explanation: Change is normal and manageable; unrecorded growth is what makes it creep.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest justification structure for an implementation method?
options: Name the safest method available
State the criteria — consequence of failure, cost, organisation size and geography, system criticality, degree of difference — evaluate, and say why the alternatives are worse
Describe all four methods in turn
Choose whichever method the client prefers
questions.explanation: The rejection of alternatives is what distinguishes justification from description.

questions.stem: A risk identified late was foreseeable at planning. The process failure is:
options: Insufficient contingency
Risk identification treated as a one-off exercise rather than a monitored, recurring activity
An incorrect risk matrix scale
Failure to transfer the risk
questions.explanation: The cycle is identify → assess → treat → monitor, with new risks feeding back into identification.

questions.stem: Which risk treatment suits a risk rated high rather than extreme?
options: Avoid by abandoning the activity
Accept and log with contingency
Reduce through controls such as testing, backups and training
Transfer entirely through insurance
questions.explanation: Extreme → avoid, high → reduce, medium → transfer, low → accept. Treating every risk as extreme consumes the capacity real extremes require.

questions.stem: Data migration should be verified by:
options: Comparing record counts and checksums, and spot-checking business-critical fields
Confirming the ETL job reported success
Checking that the source system still runs
Reviewing the migration script for syntax errors
questions.explanation: A silent partial load is the dangerous failure — job success (B) does not prove completeness.

questions.stem: Training scheduled six months before go-live is problematic because:
options: Knowledge decays before it is used, and the system will have changed
Trainers are unavailable that far ahead
It cannot be budgeted accurately
Users cannot be released from duties
questions.explanation: Just before go-live, with floor-walking support in week one, is what converts training into competence.

questions.stem: An implementation plan without go/no-go criteria means that at cutover:
options: Training cannot be scheduled
The budget cannot be reconciled
The decision to proceed becomes a judgement under pressure, with no agreed threshold or rollback trigger
The Gantt chart cannot be closed
questions.explanation: Criteria agreed in advance, when nobody is under pressure, are what make a no-go decision possible.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between the four project stages?
options: Strictly sequential with no revisiting
Iterative, with testing and evaluation findings feeding back into earlier stages
Parallel, with all four running simultaneously
Optional beyond the first two for small projects
questions.explanation: The feedback arrows are the point of the diagram, and the process diary runs across all four.

questions.stem: A team resolves conflicting stakeholder requirements by:
options: Implementing both interpretations
Deferring the requirement indefinitely
Deferring to the most senior stakeholder without discussion
Facilitating negotiation, documenting the agreed outcome and recording the rationale
questions.explanation: Negotiating is an explicitly named communication issue in this module.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence a project was cost-effective?
options: The team worked additional unpaid hours
Only open-source components were used
The client expressed satisfaction with the price
Actual versus budgeted cost, plus quantified benefit and a payback period including ongoing operating cost
questions.explanation: Cost-effectiveness is a ratio — both sides must be quantified and the denominator must include running cost.

questions.stem: A team commits to version control once weekly with the message "updates". The value lost is:
options: The ability to branch
Granular history, meaningful rollback points and a readable record of what changed and why
Off-machine backup of the code
The ability to collaborate at all
questions.explanation: The tool's benefit is proportional to the discipline applied to it.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible reason to reject a client's requested feature?
options: It conflicts with a legal or accessibility obligation, with an alternative proposed that meets the underlying goal
The team finds it technically uninteresting
It would extend the timeline
It was not in the original brief
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) are matters for negotiation; offering an alternative is what makes the refusal constructive.

questions.stem: A communication plan should specify:
options: Who is told what, through which channel, at what frequency, and who decides
The coding standards to be applied
The test data categories
The class diagram conventions
questions.explanation: It prevents stakeholders learning of problems too late and decisions being made without those who must live with them.

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes a milestone from a task?
options: A milestone has a longer duration
A milestone cannot have predecessors
A milestone is always on the critical path
A milestone marks a point in time with zero duration, usually a decision, approval or release
questions.explanation: Drawn as diamonds, milestones are the checkpoints a client's reporting usually keys to.

questions.stem: A completed system meets all requirements but usage is 15% of forecast. The most useful response is:
options: Conclude the project succeeded on its stated criteria
Add further features to attract users
Revise the usage forecast retrospectively
Investigate training, workflow fit, discoverability and trust, since adoption determines realised benefit
questions.explanation: Functional completeness without adoption produces no outcome, which is why usage belongs in the criteria set.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest indicator that requirements were poorly defined?
options: The team used prototyping
The project used an iterative approach
The client attended every review
Repeated rework caused by late discovery of what the system was actually meant to do
questions.explanation: Rework traceable to changing understanding rather than changing circumstances points back to the defining stage.

questions.stem: A team documents requirements but not the assumptions underlying them. The risk is:
options: The document becomes unwieldy
Test cases cannot be written
The client cannot approve the document
A false assumption invalidates requirements without anyone recognising why
questions.explanation: Assumptions are requirements' hidden dependencies — recording them makes their failure detectable.

questions.stem: Which best describes the purpose of a RACI matrix?
options: Ranking risks by likelihood and consequence
Documenting data items and their validation rules
Sequencing tasks and their dependencies
Identifying who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each activity
questions.explanation: Exactly one person should be Accountable — shared accountability is effectively none.

questions.stem: MoSCoW prioritisation is most useful when:
options: All requirements are equally essential
Scope must be traded against a fixed time or budget with the client
The development approach has not yet been chosen
The team is estimating task durations
questions.explanation: It converts an unstructured argument about features into a negotiation with a shared vocabulary.

questions.stem: Designing for ease of maintenance is justified because:
options: It shortens the initial build
Maintenance is typically the largest lifetime cost and is usually performed by someone other than the author
It is required for client sign-off
It improves runtime performance
questions.explanation: Modularity, meaningful naming, documentation and separated configuration all reduce total cost of ownership.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of responding appropriately to a development difficulty?
options: Silently removing the affected feature
Searching for a solution, consulting peers, considering outsourcing the specific problem, and recording the decision
Extending the deadline without consultation
Rewriting the component in an unfamiliar language
questions.explanation: These are the named strategies, and the record is assessable evidence of managed development.

questions.stem: Which pairing of testing type and purpose is correct?
options: Volume testing — confirming the interface is usable
Usability testing — verifying every code path executes
Regression testing — measuring response time under peak load
Recovery testing — restoring from backup and confirming integrity after failure
questions.explanation: (A), (C) and (B) each attach a testing type to another type's purpose.

questions.stem: A system passes UAT but fails at month-end volumes. The gap was:
options: Boundary data selection
Path testing
Accessibility testing
Volume and load testing
questions.explanation: UAT confirms fitness for purpose under normal use; peak behaviour is a separate, deliberately designed test.

questions.stem: Documentation that is subtly out of date is more dangerous than absent documentation because:
options: It is trusted, so a maintainer acts on incorrect information
It takes longer to read
It cannot be version controlled
It duplicates the code comments
questions.explanation: Change control should treat documentation as part of the deliverable rather than an afterthought.

questions.stem: In a scenario question, the highest-value action is to:
options: Define every technical term used
Reference the specific system, users, data and constraints from the stimulus in every point
List all four implementation methods before choosing
Recommend the most modern technology available
questions.explanation: Generic, technically correct answers that ignore the stimulus are the most-cited marker complaint across all four modules.

questions.stem: Which best demonstrates the evaluate verb applied to a development approach?
options: "Against the criteria of requirement stability and client availability, Agile was appropriate — requirements changed twice after sprint 2 and the client attended every review — though the fixed submission date meant scope had to be cut in sprint 4, so a WAgile approach with a fixed final increment would suit a repeat project better."
"Agile was used for this project."
"Agile is a flexible development approach."
"Agile uses sprints, stand-ups and retrospectives."
questions.explanation: Criteria, evidence both ways, a limitation, and a forward recommendation.

questions.stem: A student's project journal records only what was built each week. The improvement needed is:
options: More frequent entries
Screenshots of each completed feature
Longer entries with more technical detail
Recording decisions, their justification, problems encountered and what changed as a result
questions.explanation: The "why" entries are what earn marks for managing and evaluating development.

questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate first activity in week one of a project?
options: Selecting the front-end framework
Building the database schema
Establishing the problem definition, boundaries and measurable success criteria with the client
Drafting the user manual
questions.explanation: Every later decision depends on it, and a defect here is the most expensive kind to carry forward.

questions.stem: A structure chart shows ValidateBooking returning a true/false indicator to CreateBooking. This is drawn as:
options: An arrow with a filled circle, denoting a control flag
A hollow triangle arrow
A dashed line with no marker
A labelled rectangle between the modules
questions.explanation: Data passed down and results passed up are labelled arrows; a filled circle specifically denotes control rather than data.

questions.stem: Which statement about float is correct?
options: Every task in a project has some float
Float can be reassigned between tasks
Tasks on the critical path have zero float by definition
Float grows as the project progresses
questions.explanation: That is what makes them critical — delay propagates directly to the project end date.

questions.stem: Programmed data backup within a solution most directly supports:
options: Usability
Accessibility conformance
Business continuity and recoverability
Performance under load
questions.explanation: It links project work back to continuity planning — and an untested backup routine is not a backup.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to present the solution before final sign-off?
options: It surfaces misunderstanding while change remains possible
It demonstrates the volume of work completed
It satisfies a documentation requirement
It shortens the testing phase
questions.explanation: The value is the disagreement exposed, not the approval collected.

questions.stem: A team estimates a task at 3 days, delivers in 9, and does not update the plan. The consequence is:
options: The estimate becomes more accurate over time
The contingency budget increases automatically
Subsequent estimates and the critical path remain based on invalid data
The milestone dates recalculate themselves
questions.explanation: Planned versus actual only informs future planning if the actuals are actually recorded and used.

questions.stem: Which is the best measure of whether change control is working?
options: The number of change requests rejected
Whether each accepted change carries a documented impact assessment and approval
The speed of implementing changes
The total number of changes requested
questions.explanation: A high rejection rate (A) may indicate an inflexible process rather than a well-controlled one.

questions.stem: Which best explains why a small internal tool might use end-user development?
options: It is fast, cheap and precisely matches the user's need, with the risk contained by the tool's low criticality
It guarantees better security than professional development
It produces better documentation
It scales more easily than a professionally built system
questions.explanation: Its known weaknesses — weak validation, no version control, key-person dependency — are acceptable only where consequence of failure is low.

questions.stem: A team's velocity drops for three consecutive sprints. The most useful first response is:
options: Lengthen the sprints
Reduce the definition of done
Add developers to the team
Use the retrospective to identify the cause — blockers, technical debt, scope inflation or estimation drift
questions.explanation: (C) often slows a team further in the short term and (B) hides the problem rather than solving it.

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes user documentation from technical documentation?
options: User documentation describes how to operate the system; technical describes how it works
User documentation describes internal structure; technical describes operation
They serve the same audience at different levels of detail
Only technical documentation is required for assessment
questions.explanation: (B) is the pair inverted — both are required and they serve genuinely different readers.

questions.stem: A project's quality criteria are written after the first release. The weakness is:
options: The criteria will be too demanding
They cannot be measured
The client cannot approve them
Criteria written after the fact tend to describe what was built rather than what was needed
questions.explanation: QA requires criteria defined early and checked continually — retrospective criteria cannot do either.

questions.stem: Which best describes the purpose of a decision tree in a project context?
options: Sequencing dependent tasks and computing float
Capturing business rules and eligibility logic for client confirmation before implementation
Documenting data movement between processes
Showing class inheritance relationships
questions.explanation: It makes branching logic reviewable by a non-technical stakeholder while it is still cheap to change.

questions.stem: A team cannot decide between two designs. The most defensible resolution is:
options: Prototype both cheaply and test with representative users against the agreed criteria
Choose the one the most senior developer prefers
Implement both and remove one later
Defer the decision until after implementation
questions.explanation: Design thinking's test stage exists precisely to resolve disagreements with evidence rather than seniority.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to record the reasoning behind a rejected option?
options: It lengthens the project documentation
It satisfies a version control requirement
It prevents the same option being re-proposed and re-analysed, and supports later evaluation of the decision
It demonstrates the volume of analysis performed
questions.explanation: Decision records are as valuable for what was rejected as for what was chosen.

questions.stem: A stimulus describes a system where failure would prevent legally required reporting during a two-week window. The conversion method should be:
options: Direct, scheduled inside the window
Phased across the reporting modules
Pilot with the reporting team
Parallel, or the cutover moved outside the window
questions.explanation: Both timing and fallback matter — the same system might justify direct cutover in a quiet period.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest example of preventive maintenance?
options: Updating a library before a known vulnerability is exploited
Correcting a defect reported by a user
Adding a report requested after launch
Adjusting the system for a legislative change
questions.explanation: (B) corrective, (C) perfective, (D) adaptive — the category most often cut from budgets and most reliably regretted.

questions.stem: A team wants evidence that its solution is accessible. The strongest is:
options: The developers reviewed it for accessibility
The colour palette was chosen carefully
A WCAG conformance audit plus testing with keyboard-only and screen-reader users
The site uses semantic HTML throughout
questions.explanation: (D) is a good practice and contributes, but conformance plus real assistive-technology testing is the evidence.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between risk management and implementation method?
options: They are independent project decisions
Risk management applies only after go-live
The implementation method is set by the budget alone
The assessed consequence of failure drives the choice, pushing high-consequence systems toward parallel or phased
questions.explanation: Making that link explicit is what turns a description of four methods into a justification.

questions.stem: A team ships a feature that satisfies the written requirement but not the client's evident intent. The correct response is:
options: Raise the divergence, clarify the intent, and process the correction through change control
Point to the written requirement and close the item
Rewrite the requirement retrospectively to match what was built
Absorb the rework silently
questions.explanation: (B) is technically defensible and professionally corrosive; (C) destroys the traceability the requirement existed to provide.

questions.stem: Which is the most useful measure of documentation quality?
options: Its length and level of detail
Whether someone other than the author can complete real tasks using it
Whether it covers every function in the codebase
Whether it was written before implementation
questions.explanation: Trialling the documentation is an explicit syllabus requirement precisely because authors cannot see their own assumptions.

questions.stem: A project uses collaboration tools but decisions are made in ad-hoc conversations. The consequence is:
options: Faster decision-making with less overhead
No audit trail, so the reasoning behind decisions is lost and disputes cannot be resolved
The tools become redundant
Version control conflicts increase
questions.explanation: The audit trail is the named benefit of collaboration tooling — it only exists if decisions are recorded there.

questions.stem: Which is the best justification for choosing prototyping for a customer-facing interface?
options: It is the cheapest approach available
It removes the need for testing
The requirements are interface-centred and partly unarticulated, so users reacting to something tangible elicits what interviews would miss
It guarantees the delivery date
questions.explanation: Then say why not waterfall (requirements unstable) and why not end-user development (customer-facing, security relevant).

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports a claim that the solution solved the original problem?
options: A demonstration of every implemented feature
Each original measurable criterion reported against the achieved result
A list of technologies and libraries used
The client's written thanks
questions.explanation: Closing the loop back to the problem definition is what converts a description into an evaluation.

questions.stem: A team treats testing as a phase performed only after all code is complete. The most likely consequence is:
options: Defects discovered late, when they are most expensive to fix, with insufficient time to remediate
Higher code quality through focused effort
Better test coverage
Reduced documentation burden
questions.explanation: Continuous testing from the start is the same shift-left argument that drives secure development.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest indicator that a project's estimates were realistic?
options: The project finished early
Actuals tracked close to estimates, and variances were investigated and explained
No task exceeded its estimate
The contingency was never used
questions.explanation: Consistently unused contingency (D) and no overruns at all (C) can indicate padded estimates rather than accurate ones.

questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate use of outsourcing in a student or small project?
options: Bringing in specific outside expertise for a discrete technical problem, and documenting the decision
Outsourcing the entire build to reduce workload
Outsourcing the requirements gathering
Outsourcing the evaluation
questions.explanation: It is named as a strategy for responding to development difficulties, not a delivery model for the whole project.

questions.stem: A class diagram omits methods and shows only attributes. The consequence is:
options: The behaviour of each class is undocumented, so the diagram supports data design but not interaction design
The diagram is invalid notation
Inheritance cannot be represented
The diagram cannot be used for implementation
questions.explanation: The three compartments — name, attributes, methods — each carry distinct information.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument for involving end users rather than only the client in design?
options: The client's picture of daily workflow is often incomplete, and users reveal needs a specification would miss
End users are easier to schedule
End users approve the budget
It shortens the requirements phase
questions.explanation: It is the practical defence against a system that verifies perfectly and validates poorly.

questions.stem: A project's risk register lists risks but records no owners or review dates. The weakness is:
options: The register is too long
The likelihood scale is undefined
Without ownership and review, risks are identified but never actively monitored or treated
The register duplicates the issue log
questions.explanation: Monitor is the fourth step of the cycle — a register that is written once is documentation, not risk management.

questions.stem: Which best describes why verification and validation are both required?
options: They are alternative names for the same activity
Verification confirms the build matches the specification; validation confirms the specification was the right one
Verification is automated and validation is manual
Verification applies to code and validation to documentation
questions.explanation: A system can fully satisfy the first and completely fail the second — which is why UAT sits opposite the problem definition in the V-model.

questions.stem: A team must communicate the solution to four audiences. The best approach is:
options: Produce one comprehensive document covering everything
Provide a demonstration video only
Present the technical documentation to all four
Match the artefact and vocabulary to each audience — executives, end users, maintainers and the public
questions.explanation: Communicating to a specific audience is an assessed outcome, and one artefact rarely serves four purposes well.

questions.stem: Which statement about the process diary is most accurate?
options: It should be written at the end of the project from memory
It replaces the need for a Gantt chart
It runs across all four stages and its value lies in dated decisions and their justification
It records only technical activity
questions.explanation: It is the primary evidence for recording management and evaluating development.

questions.stem: A team discovers during testing that a core assumption was wrong. The correct response is:
options: Complete the current build and note the issue in the final report
Feed the finding back into defining and planning, revise the affected design, and re-test
Adjust the test to match the implemented behaviour
Reduce the scope to exclude the affected area
questions.explanation: The iterative feedback path is exactly what the four-stage diagram's return arrows represent.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a quality criterion as distinct from a functional requirement?
options: "Users can export a report to PDF"
"Administrators can reset a user's password"
"The system stores customer contact details"
"All pages meet WCAG 2.1 AA and load within 2 seconds at the 95th percentile"
questions.explanation: Quality criteria are the measurable standards the delivered functionality must meet.

questions.stem: A team reduces an estimate because the client objects to it. The consequence is:
options: A plan that silently guarantees an overrun, moving the problem to where it costs more
A more efficient schedule
A shorter critical path
An increase in available float
questions.explanation: Negotiate the scope, not the number — the estimate is a forecast, not an opening position.

questions.stem: Which best explains why documentation should be updated as part of a change?
options: Documentation that no longer matches the system is trusted and therefore actively misleading
It is required by version control tooling
It increases the change's traceability score
It shortens the regression test cycle
questions.explanation: Treating documentation as part of the deliverable rather than an afterthought is what prevents this drift.

questions.stem: A stimulus describes a low-risk internal tool, a tight budget and a small user group. The best-matched implementation method is:
options: Parallel across all users
Direct cutover
Pilot across three groups
Phased over six months
questions.explanation: Right-sizing the method to the risk is the judgement being tested — the same reasoning that rules direct cutover out for payroll.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that feedback influenced the solution?
options: Feedback was collected from a representative group
Feedback was summarised in the final report
Feedback was recorded verbatim in the diary
A documented change traceable to specific feedback, followed by re-testing
questions.explanation: Collection is the easy half — the loop closes with the change and its verification.

questions.stem: A team must choose between building a feature and buying a component. The decisive criterion is usually:
options: Which option is cheaper in the first year
Which option the vendor recommends
Which option uses newer technology
Whether the capability is core to the solution's value and whether the team can maintain it
questions.explanation: First-year cost systematically favours buying and ignores lock-in and fit, which is why it is a poor sole criterion.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of technical debt in a student project?
options: Money owed for software licences
Shortcuts taken to meet a deadline that increase the cost of future change
Features deferred to a later release
Defects found during testing
questions.explanation: Recognising and recording it — rather than pretending it does not exist — is what makes the trade-off deliberate.

questions.stem: A project's evaluation reports only strengths. The weakness is:
options: Evaluate, assess and discuss verbs require balanced consideration of limitations before a judgement
It is too short to be credible
It should be written by the client
It duplicates the testing report
questions.explanation: An evaluation with no limitations reads as advocacy rather than assessment.

questions.stem: Which testing activity most directly addresses the requirement to "compare actual output with expected output"?
options: Usability testing
Penetration testing
Executing documented test cases with defined expected results
Load testing
questions.explanation: It is the fundamental test of correctness, and it requires the expected result to have been documented in advance.

questions.stem: A team plans to demonstrate the solution using presentation software. The most important preparation is:
options: Ensuring the slides use the organisation's template
Including the full technical architecture
Framing the demonstration around the client's stated criteria and the decisions they need to make
Rehearsing the feature list in order
questions.explanation: Communicating to a specific audience means leading with the outcome, not the process.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to keep the raw project data — estimates, test results, feedback — rather than only the summary?
options: It increases the volume of the submission
It satisfies a version control requirement
It allows conclusions to be traced back to evidence and re-examined
It demonstrates the effort expended
questions.explanation: Traceability from claim to evidence is what makes an evaluation assessable rather than assertive.

questions.stem: A project's final system is functional, documented and evaluated, but no version history exists. The most significant loss is:
options: The ability to demonstrate the solution
The ability to conduct UAT
The ability to write user documentation
Evidence of the development process, plus the ability to roll back or trace when a change was made
questions.explanation: Version control is both a technical tool and assessable evidence of managed development.

questions.stem: Which best captures the purpose of the testing and evaluating stage?
options: To confirm the system compiles and runs
To produce the user documentation
To establish whether the system works correctly and whether it meets the need, then feed findings back
To obtain client sign-off
questions.explanation: Verification, validation and the feedback loop — sign-off is a consequence rather than the purpose.

questions.stem: A team is asked to "assess" its choice of development approach. The answer must:
options: Describe the approach and its stages
Weigh its value and significance for this project, with evidence, and reach a verdict
Compare all five approaches equally
Recommend a different approach for next time only
questions.explanation: Assess demands a judgement about value or significance — description caps at the lower bands.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible way to handle a requirement that cannot be delivered within the timeframe?
options: Deliver a partial implementation without telling the client
Extend the deadline unilaterally
Raise it early, propose descoping or phasing with a rationale, and record the agreed decision
Deliver it untested to meet the date
questions.explanation: Early disclosure preserves the client's options; late disclosure removes them.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between the process diary and the final evaluation?
options: They are independent documents serving different assessors
The evaluation replaces the diary at project end
The diary supplies the dated evidence — decisions, problems, feedback and changes — that the evaluation draws on
The diary is written from the evaluation
questions.explanation: An evaluation without an evidence trail is assertion; the diary is where that trail is built as the project runs.

questions.stem: Taken together, which body of evidence best demonstrates professional practice across a completed project?
options: A technically sophisticated finished product
Use of the most current frameworks and libraries
Completion ahead of the scheduled date
Planned versus actual tracking, version control history, documented decisions with reasoning, criteria-based evaluation and demonstrated response to feedback
questions.explanation: These are exactly what the outcomes ask you to apply methods to manage, document and evaluate — assessable in a way a finished artefact alone is not.
